team. But here's the catch. It's not

Sales, marketing, maybe even someone
there from legal to veto everything.

departments. They have different

it may not even be officially labeled as
a team. Instead, it might have been
given some vague term like project
committee or task force. You have a
shared goal for the project, but you
have no shared history, no shared
habits. You don't even know if you can

the challenge and the opportunity of
managing a crossf functional team. If

In theory, crossunctional teams are
supposed to help organizations move
faster, break silos, be more innovative.
But in reality, most crossfunctional
teams are actually stuck. In fact, in
one study, 75% of crossf functional
teams were found to be dysfunctional
teams, meaning they struggled to stay on
schedule to meet their budget or even
keep the team in alignment with the
organization's goals. Now, this
dysfunction isn't necessarily because
the people on the team aren't talented.
It's actually because most people, most
teams don't take the time to build the
structure these talented people need to
collaborate well across all those
different departments. It's a common
mistake when people get asked to lead a
crossunctional team. They start to focus
on the work itself. There's a deadline
to meet after all. And so they start
scheduling meetings and assigning tasks
and setting everything up based on what
needs to be done, but don't take the
time to talk about the people doing it.
And when you don't make an effort to
create communication norms, make sure
our goals are aligned or create role
clarity among the team, then everyone
starts to default back to their habits,
the way they were trained in their own
little silo. And all that great stuff,

before you start tossing out tasks, you
need to make sure everyone is clear
around two fundamental questions. What
are we trying to achieve? and who is
doing what to get us there.
The beauty of crossf functional teams is
that everybody brings something a little
bit different. Different skills,
different perspectives, different
backgrounds. The challenge is that
nobody knows what everybody brings and
so nobody knows who's best suited for
what. As a leader, creating that
clarity, that's your first step. For
some project tasks, the owner will be

people might both think they're the best
suited for it, or nobody steps up right

someone might volunteer for a stretch

they're best suited for something that

We all know that good communication can
make or break a team. But this is where
many crossunctional teams get messed up.
People come from different backgrounds,
different training, different norms
inside their departments. and all of
them think that their norm is the best
way to do things. So, we need to come
together to have a conversation about
what the new norms specific to this team
are. During your first meeting as a team
or during the project kickoff, you're
going to want to have a conversation
about those communication norms. The way
I do this is I start with a list of
questions. Questions designed to get a
feel for what everyone's background is
and then what we as a team are going to
do. Here's a few questions to get you
started. How should people keep each
other updated on progress? What mediums
of communication should the team use and
for what purpose? How should we make
requests for help? How does the team
want to give each other feedback? How
often should we be having meetings? How
will decisions be made? Once you've
agreed to the answers to all of these
questions, take the time to document
them and put that somewhere accessible,
somewhere where everybody can see it.
That way, everyone's on the same page
about how they're supposed to show up in
meetings, how they're supposed to speak
up, how they're supposed to communicate
with each other, and what tools they're
supposed to use, and if or when the
workflow starts to trip up, you've got
that set of norms you can point back to

Communication norms are essential, but
communication alone does not build a
great team. You're going to want to
develop a sense of empathy on the team
or what I call common understanding.
Think about it. You've got all these
people from different backgrounds who
were trained to think differently. And
unless you understand how they think,
when you try and communicate with them,
you're going to end up talking past
them. The good news is that empathy can
be built. Start by having everyone on
the team share a bit more about them.
Not just their role, but what does
success look like for them in their home
department. How is their boss judging
their performance? How much time is
their boss letting them give to this
project? And what about this project is
going to help them look like a superstar
back in their regular department. When
people understand each other's goals and
thought processes, that crossunctional
magic you're looking for becomes
reality. And when problems arise, and
problems will arise, they arise on any
team, you'll have the context and the
understanding of other people's thinking
to find solutions that work for
everyone.
And speaking of conflict, you might find

we're going to need to build what

In short, it means creating a culture of
cander where people feel like they can

opening the door for that feedback. And
when that feedback comes in, you're

pretty toxic level of conflict. For
example, and here's one of my favorite
tips. When somebody is either pushing

their idea and you don't agree with it,
make sure you are not questioning the
idea itself or questioning the

both acting logically from a different

Big projects can feel overwhelming and
especially on a cross functional team
when people are juggling all sorts of
other projects. It can be really easy to
think the one with the far off vague
deadline is the one I'm going to spend
the least amount of time on. That's why
crossf functional teams need
checkpoints. They need milestones that
let the team know, hey, we are making
progress toward this goal. What do those
milestones look like? Well, it depends
on the project, but start by breaking it
up into phases. If this is the goal for
our 2-year long project, what does the
next month look like, the next quarter,
the next 6 months, the next year? How
will we know we're making progress? This
not only helps keep the team accountable
and let them know if they need to pivot
anything, but it helps build a sense of
accomplishment along the way, like
things are working, we are working well
as a team. And when you do hit those
milestones, celebrate it. Research
suggests that celebrating even the
smallest wins, even if it's a quick
thank you in an email or a shout out in
a meeting, celebrating those smallest
wins can have a dramatic impact on the
team's morale and boost their
performance over time. The trick is to
celebrate these wins often, but not so
often that it comes off as fake or
inauthentic. You don't need to shout
someone out every single meeting just
because you do it every meeting, but
anytime there is a win, make sure the
team knows about it. All right, we've
